title: Selecting, Filtering & Aggregating
description: The everyday pandas moves: picking exactly the rows and columns you need, building new columns, and summarizing data by group.

lessons.title: Selecting Rows and Columns
lessons.description: Learn the core ways to grab exactly the data you need out of a DataFrame.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can select specific columns and rows from a DataFrame using label-based and position-based indexing.

sections.title: 📌 Selecting columns
sections.content:
Select one column with square brackets and its name; select several with a list of names.

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Ana", "Bo", "Chen"],
    "age": [25, 31, 42],
    "city": ["Lahore", "Karachi", "Lahore"],
})

print(df["age"])              # single column → Series
print(df[["name", "age"]])    # multiple columns → DataFrame
```

sections.title: 🏷️ .loc: selecting by label
sections.content:
`.loc` selects rows and columns **by label** — the actual index value or column name.

```python
print(df.loc[0])                 # the row with index label 0
print(df.loc[0, "name"])         # "Ana"
print(df.loc[0:1, ["name", "age"]])  # rows 0-1, two columns
```

sections.title: 🔢 .iloc: selecting by position
sections.content:
`.iloc` selects **by integer position**, regardless of what the labels actually are — useful when you just want "the first 3 rows" or "the second column."

```python
print(df.iloc[0])          # first row, by position
print(df.iloc[0:2])        # first two rows
print(df.iloc[:, 1])       # second column, all rows
```

• `.loc` uses labels (what things are *called*)
• `.iloc` uses positions (where things *are*)

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Mixing up `.loc` and `.iloc`.** `.loc[0:2]` (label-based) includes the endpoint; `.iloc[0:2]` (position-based) does not — a classic off-by-one trap.

**Forgetting single-column selection returns a Series, not a DataFrame.** `df["age"]` and `df[["age"]]` look similar but return different types.

**Assuming row labels are always 0, 1, 2...** After filtering or sorting, the index can have gaps — `.iloc` still works by position, but `.loc` won't find a label that's no longer there.

questions.question: What's the key difference between `.loc` and `.iloc`?
options: There is no difference — they're interchangeable
`.loc` selects by label, `.iloc` selects by integer position
`.loc` only works on columns, `.iloc` only on rows
questions.explanation: `.loc` looks up rows/columns by their actual label (index value or column name), while `.iloc` looks them up by numeric position, regardless of the label.

questions.question: What does `df["age"]` return?
questions.explanation: Selecting a single column with square brackets and its name returns a Series — a one-dimensional labeled array.

questions.question: Why might `.loc[0]` fail to find a row after filtering the DataFrame?
options: Filtering can remove the row with index label 0, so that label no longer exists
questions.explanation: After filtering, the original index labels are preserved on the remaining rows — so a label like 0 might have been filtered out entirely, making `.loc[0]` raise an error.

questions.question: How do you select multiple specific columns from a DataFrame at once?
options: df[['col1', 'col2']] — passing a list of column names
questions.explanation: Passing a list of column names inside the square brackets, like df[['col1', 'col2']], selects multiple columns and returns a DataFrame.

questions.question: How does `.iloc[2:5]` behave when slicing rows?
options: It selects rows labeled 2 through 5, inclusive
It selects rows at positions 2, 3, and 4 (position-based, end-exclusive, like standard Python slicing)
It selects exactly 5 rows starting from the top
It raises an error since iloc doesn't support slicing
questions.explanation: `.iloc` uses integer position, so `2:5` follows normal Python slice rules — it grabs positions 2, 3, and 4, excluding position 5.

questions.question: How would you select a single value at row label 3, column 'price' using `.loc`?
questions.explanation: `.loc` accepts a row label and column label together, like df.loc[3, 'price'], to pinpoint a single value.

questions.question: What is the key difference between `df['col']` and `df[['col']]` when selecting a column?
options: `df['col']` returns a Series; `df[['col']]` returns a single-column DataFrame
questions.explanation: Single brackets with a plain column name give back a Series, while a list of column names (even one) gives back a DataFrame.

questions.question: How would you select columns 'name' through 'age' (inclusive) by their position order using `.loc`?
options: df.loc[:, 'name':'age'] — label-based slicing includes both endpoints
questions.explanation: `.loc` supports label-based slicing across columns, and unlike `.iloc`, the end label is included in the result.

lessons.title: Filtering Rows with Conditions
lessons.description: Learn how to keep only the rows that match a condition — one of the most common operations in data work.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can filter a DataFrame down to rows matching one or more conditions.

sections.title: ✅ Boolean masks
sections.content:
Writing a condition on a DataFrame produces a **boolean mask** — a Series of True/False values, one per row. Passing that mask back into the DataFrame keeps only the True rows.

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Ana", "Bo", "Chen"],
    "age": [25, 31, 42],
})

mask = df["age"] > 30
print(mask)          # [False, True, True]
print(df[mask])      # only Bo and Chen
print(df[df["age"] > 30])  # same thing, written directly
```

sections.title: 🔗 Combining conditions
sections.content:
Combine multiple conditions with `&` (and), `|` (or), and `~` (not) — each condition needs its own parentheses.

```python
older_from_lahore = df[(df["age"] > 30) & (df["city"] == "Lahore")]
not_from_lahore = df[~(df["city"] == "Lahore")]
```

• Use `&`, `|`, `~` — not Python's `and`, `or`, `not`, which don't work element-wise on a Series
• Always parenthesize each individual condition

sections.title: 🔎 Filtering with .isin() and string matching
sections.content:
Two very common filtering patterns:

```python
# Match against a list of allowed values
df[df["city"].isin(["Lahore", "Karachi"])]

# Match rows where a text column contains a substring
df[df["name"].str.contains("an", case=False)]
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Using `and`/`or` instead of `&`/`|`.** Python's built-in boolean operators don't work element-wise across a Series and will raise an error.

**Forgetting parentheses around each condition.** `df[df.age > 30 & df.city == "Lahore"]` breaks due to operator precedence — wrap each comparison in its own parentheses.

**Filtering and forgetting the result is a new DataFrame.** `df[mask]` doesn't change `df` — assign the result to a new variable if you want to keep it.

questions.question: What does `df[df["age"] > 30]` return?
options: A new DataFrame containing only rows where age is greater than 30
questions.explanation: The condition creates a boolean mask, and indexing the DataFrame with that mask returns only the rows where the condition was True.

questions.question: Why can't you use Python's `and` to combine two pandas conditions?
options: `and` doesn't work element-wise across a Series of True/False values — `&` is needed instead
questions.explanation: Python's `and`/`or` expect single boolean values, not element-wise arrays — pandas requires `&`, `|`, and `~` for combining conditions across a Series.

questions.question: What does `df["city"].isin(["Lahore", "Karachi"])` check?
options: Whether the city column exactly equals a single string
Whether each row's city value is one of the values in the given list
Whether the DataFrame contains a column called Lahore
Nothing — isin() is not a real method
questions.explanation: `.isin()` returns True for rows whose value in that column matches any value in the provided list — handy for filtering against multiple allowed values at once.

questions.question: How would you filter rows where age is over 30 OR city is 'Lahore'?
questions.explanation: The `|` operator performs element-wise OR across boolean Series, matching rows where either condition holds.

questions.question: How do you select rows where a condition is NOT true, like excluding a particular city?
options: Using the `not` keyword directly on the Series
Using the `~` operator to negate a boolean mask, like df[~(df['city'] == 'Lahore')]
Using `!=` is never valid for this
questions.explanation: The `~` operator negates a boolean Series element-wise, letting you flip a condition to select everything that does NOT match.

questions.question: How would you filter rows where a text column contains a certain substring?
questions.explanation: `.str.contains()` checks each row's string for a substring match, letting you filter based on partial text rather than an exact match.

questions.question: Why might chaining several filter conditions together in one line need extra parentheses around each condition?
options: Parentheses are purely stylistic and never required
Python's operator precedence can otherwise misinterpret where one comparison ends and the next combining operator begins
Pandas doesn't allow multiple conditions at all
Only two conditions can ever be combined
questions.explanation: Because comparison and bitwise operators have different precedence than expected, wrapping each condition in parentheses avoids Python misgrouping the expression.

questions.question: What's a common mistake when combining multiple filter conditions with `&`?
options: Using `&` at all, since it's always wrong
Forgetting to wrap each individual condition in parentheses, which causes a precedence error
questions.explanation: Without parentheses around each comparison, Python's operator precedence rules can misinterpret the combined expression, so `(cond1) & (cond2)` is the safe pattern.

lessons.title: Creating and Transforming Columns
lessons.description: Learn how to add new columns computed from existing ones — the heart of feature building.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can create new columns from existing ones using direct math and the `.apply()` method.

sections.title: ➕ Creating columns with vectorized math
sections.content:
Assigning to a new column name creates it. Operations on whole columns happen **element-wise** — no manual loop needed.

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"price": [10, 20, 30], "quantity": [2, 1, 5]})

df["total"] = df["price"] * df["quantity"]
print(df)
#    price  quantity  total
# 0     10         2     20
# 1     20         1     20
# 2     30         5    150
```

This vectorized style is both simpler to read and much faster than looping row by row in Python.

sections.title: 🧠 Custom logic with .apply()
sections.content:
For logic too complex for simple math, `.apply()` runs a function on every value (or every row).

```python
def price_tier(price):
    if price < 15:
        return "low"
    elif price < 25:
        return "medium"
    return "high"

df["tier"] = df["price"].apply(price_tier)
```

`.apply()` is flexible but slower than vectorized math — reach for direct column operations first, and `.apply()` when the logic genuinely needs it.

sections.title: 🔁 A handy shortcut: np.where
sections.content:
For simple if/else logic on a whole column, `numpy`'s `where` is a fast, readable alternative to `.apply()`.

```python
import numpy as np

df["is_bulk"] = np.where(df["quantity"] >= 5, True, False)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Looping over rows with a `for` loop instead of using vectorized operations.** It works, but it's dramatically slower on real-sized data and usually a sign there's a simpler pandas way.

**Overusing `.apply()` for logic that vectorized math could handle.** If it's a comparison or arithmetic, direct column math is faster and clearer.

**Forgetting new columns need to be assigned, not just computed.** `df["price"] * df["quantity"]` alone just prints a Series — it needs `df["total"] = ...` to actually save it.

questions.question: What does `df["total"] = df["price"] * df["quantity"]` do?
options: Prints the multiplication result without saving it
Creates a new column called total holding the element-wise product of price and quantity
Raises an error since columns can't be multiplied
Deletes the price and quantity columns
questions.explanation: Assigning the result of an element-wise operation to a new column name both computes and stores it as a new column in the DataFrame.

questions.question: When should you prefer `.apply()` over direct vectorized math?
options: When the logic is too complex for simple arithmetic or comparisons
Only when working with text columns
questions.explanation: Vectorized math is faster and simpler for arithmetic/comparisons; `.apply()` earns its slower performance cost when the logic is genuinely more complex, like custom conditional branching.

questions.question: Why is looping over DataFrame rows with a plain Python `for` loop usually discouraged?
options: Vectorized operations achieve the same result and are typically much faster
It only works on the first row
questions.explanation: Pandas is built around vectorized (whole-column) operations, which are implemented efficiently — row-by-row Python loops are much slower on real datasets.

questions.question: How would you create a column that's 'high' or 'low' based on whether price exceeds 100, without using `.apply()`?
options: Only .apply() can do conditional column creation
questions.explanation: np.where(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false) is a fast, vectorized way to create a conditional column without the overhead of .apply().

questions.question: How do you modify an existing column's values in place, like converting a text column to uppercase?
options: This requires a for loop over every row
questions.explanation: Reassigning the transformed values back to the same column name, like df['col'] = df['col'].str.upper(), updates the column with the new values.

questions.question: How would you create a new column extracting the first word from a text column?
options: df['col'].split(' ')[0] applied directly to the whole column
This isn't possible without a manual loop
questions.explanation: Using `.str.split()` to break each string into parts, then `.str[0]` to grab the first element, works element-wise across the whole column.

questions.question: Why do vectorized operations like `df['a'] * df['b']` avoid the need for an explicit Python loop?
options: They secretly run a loop internally that's just hidden from you, with no speed benefit
They apply the operation to every row at once using optimized, compiled code under the hood, rather than looping in Python
Vectorized operations only work on a single row at a time
They only work on text columns
questions.explanation: Vectorized operations push the looping down into fast, compiled code rather than Python's slower interpreted loop, applying the operation to the whole column at once.

questions.question: When is using `.apply()` for a column overkill compared to plain vectorized math?
options: When the transformation is a simple arithmetic operation, like adding two numeric columns together
When the logic genuinely requires row-by-row custom decisions that can't be expressed as simple arithmetic
questions.explanation: If the goal is simple arithmetic like df['a'] + df['b'], reaching for .apply() with a custom function is unnecessary and slower than plain vectorized math.

lessons.title: GroupBy: Aggregating Data by Category
lessons.description: Learn the split-apply-combine pattern that powers almost every summary table you'll ever build.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can group data by a category and compute summary statistics per group.

sections.title: ✂️ Split-apply-combine
sections.content:
`groupby` follows a three-step pattern:

• **Split** the data into groups based on a column's values
• **Apply** an aggregation function (like sum, mean, count) to each group
• **Combine** the results back into a single table

This single pattern covers an enormous range of everyday questions: "average order size per city", "total sales per month", "count of customers per plan type."

sections.title: 📊 A basic groupby
sections.content:
```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Lahore", "Karachi", "Lahore", "Karachi"],
    "sales": [100, 150, 200, 50],
})

result = df.groupby("city")["sales"].sum()
print(result)
# city
# Karachi    200
# Lahore     300
# Name: sales, dtype: int64
```

The result's index becomes the group labels.

sections.title: 🧮 Multiple aggregations at once
sections.content:
Use `.agg()` to compute several statistics per group in one call.

```python
summary = df.groupby("city")["sales"].agg(["sum", "mean", "count"])
print(summary)
#          sum   mean  count
# city
# Karachi  200  100.0      2
# Lahore   300  150.0      2
```

You can also group by multiple columns at once by passing a list: `df.groupby(["city", "month"])`.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Forgetting to select a column before aggregating.** `df.groupby("city").sum()` sums every numeric column — usually you want `df.groupby("city")["sales"].sum()` for just the one you care about.

**Assuming groupby preserves original row order.** The result is organized by group label, not by the order rows appeared in the original data.

**Grouping by a column with too many unique values.** Grouping by something like a raw customer ID often produces a group of size one per row — not a useful summary.

questions.question: What are the three steps in the groupby pattern?
questions.explanation: Groupby splits data into groups by a key, applies an aggregation to each group, then combines the results into one summary table.

questions.question: What does `df.groupby("city")["sales"].sum()` compute?
options: The total sales across the whole dataset, ignoring city
The total sales, summed separately for each unique city
The number of cities in the dataset
The average sale price per transaction
questions.explanation: This groups rows by the city column, then sums the sales column within each group — giving one total per city.

questions.question: What does `.agg(["sum", "mean", "count"])` let you do?
options: Compute only the sum, ignoring the other names
Compute multiple summary statistics for each group in a single call
Filter out groups with fewer than 3 rows
questions.explanation: `.agg()` accepts a list of aggregation functions and computes all of them per group, returning them as separate columns in the result.

questions.question: How would you group by both 'region' and 'category' at once?
options: This requires two separate groupby calls chained without a list
questions.explanation: Passing a list of column names to groupby(), like ['region', 'category'], groups by the unique combinations of both columns.

questions.question: What's the difference between `.size()` and `.count()` after a groupby?
options: `.size()` counts all rows per group including missing values; `.count()` counts only non-missing values per column per group
`.size()` only works on the whole DataFrame, not after groupby
questions.explanation: `.size()` gives the raw row count per group regardless of missing data, while `.count()` counts non-null values separately for each column.

questions.question: Why would you call `.reset_index()` after a groupby aggregation?
options: It converts the grouped column (which became the index) back into a regular column, useful for further processing or merging
It's required before groupby can run at all
questions.explanation: After a groupby aggregation, the grouping column becomes the index; `.reset_index()` turns it back into an ordinary column, which is often more convenient.

questions.question: How would you compute the average sale amount per city?
questions.explanation: Grouping by 'city' and calling .mean() on the 'sales' column computes the average sales value separately within each city group.

questions.question: Why is `groupby` generally preferred over manually looping through each unique category value?
options: Looping through unique values is actually faster
groupby handles the splitting, computing, and recombining internally using optimized code, avoiding slow, error-prone manual loops
groupby can only be used with numeric data
Manual loops are required for any aggregation
questions.explanation: groupby implements the split-apply-combine pattern efficiently under the hood, sparing you from writing and debugging a manual loop over every unique category.
